question: When can palliative care be initiated for a patient with a life-threatening illness?

options.A: Only after curative treatments have stopped
options.B: At the time of diagnosis, alongside curative treatments
options.C: Only during the final 24 hours of life

explanation: Palliative care can be initiated at the time of diagnosis and provided alongside curative treatments to manage symptoms and distress. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T2#GNS221_U4_T2_h1)

question: What is the primary focus of end-of-life nursing care?

options.A: Finding a cure for the terminal disease
options.D: Restricting family visits to reduce stress

explanation: The core philosophy of end-of-life care centers on maximizing patient comfort, preserving dignity, and supporting the family. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T2#GNS221_U4_T2_h1)

question: What causes the characteristic 'death rattle' sound in a dying patient?

options.B: Accumulation of oral and pharyngeal secretions

explanation: The 'death rattle' is caused by an accumulation of oral and pharyngeal secretions that the patient is no longer able to clear. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T2#GNS221_U4_T2_h2)

question: Which sensory function is widely believed to remain intact until the very end of life?
explanation: Hearing is widely believed to remain intact until the very end of life, which is why nurses should encourage families to keep talking to the patient. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T2#GNS221_U4_T2_h2)

question: How should a nurse assess pain in a dying patient who is non-verbal and unresponsive?

options.A: Wait until the patient wakes up to ask
options.B: Rely on validated behavioral pain scales and observe for physical signs like grimacing
options.C: Assume the patient is in no pain if they cannot speak

explanation: When patients are non-verbal, nurses use validated behavioral pain scales and observe for non-verbal cues such as grimacing or restlessness. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T2#GNS221_U4_T2_h3)

question: What is a potential negative consequence of forced aggressive hydration in an actively dying patient?

options.A: Rapid recovery from the terminal illness

explanation: Aggressive hydration in dying patients can lead to fluid overload, causing respiratory congestion, pulmonary edema, and increased discomfort. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T2#GNS221_U4_T2_h3)

question: Which pharmacological class is primarily used for the management of severe pain at the end of life?
explanation: Opioids are the cornerstone of pharmacological pain management for severe pain in end-of-life care. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T2#GNS221_U4_T2_h4)

question: What is a helpful non-pharmacological measure to alleviate dyspnea in a dying patient?

options.A: Placing the patient flat on their back
options.B: Elevating the head of the bed

explanation: Elevating the head of the bed helps ease breathing and reduces the sensation of dyspnea in terminal patients. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T2#GNS221_U4_T2_h4)

question: What type of grief do family members typically experience while watching their loved one decline?
explanation: Anticipatory grief occurs when family members experience emotional distress and mourning prior to the actual death of their loved one. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T2#GNS221_U4_T2_h5)

question: Why is facilitating spiritual support important during end-of-life care?

options.A: It replaces the need for medical pain management
options.B: It addresses existential distress and aligns with cultural or religious beliefs
options.C: It speeds up the dying process
options.D: It is a mandatory legal requirement in all hospitals

explanation: Spiritual support helps address existential distress and respects the patient and family's cultural and religious values. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T2#GNS221_U4_T2_h5)

question: Which ethical principle upholds a competent patient's right to make their own healthcare decisions?
explanation: Autonomy refers to the right of competent individuals to make decisions about their own medical treatment and care. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T2#GNS221_U4_T2_h6)

question: What is the primary legal and ethical distinction regarding palliative sedation at the end of life?

options.A: Its goal is to hasten the patient's death
options.B: Its intent is to relieve refractory physical suffering
options.C: It is legally classified as active euthanasia
options.D: It can be initiated without family or patient consent

explanation: Palliative sedation is ethically and legally distinct because its sole intent is to relieve severe, refractory suffering rather than to hasten death. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T2#GNS221_U4_T2_h6)

question: How should a nurse position a deceased patient during post-mortem care?

options.A: In a sitting position with knees bent
options.B: Supine with arms straight or across the abdomen and a pillow under the head
options.C: Prone with the face turned to the side
options.D: In a semi-Fowler's position at 45 degrees

explanation: During post-mortem care, the body is positioned supine with a pillow under the head to prevent blood pooling and discoloration in the face. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T2#GNS221_U4_T2_h7)

question: What is an important nursing responsibility immediately following a patient's death regarding the family?

options.A: Rushing them to clear the room for a new admission
options.B: Allowing private time to view the body and perform cultural mourning rituals
options.C: Discouraging any emotional expression to maintain hospital quietness
options.D: Asking them to assist with washing the body for the morgue

explanation: Nurses must provide families with private time to view the body and carry out necessary cultural or religious mourning rites. [learn more](GNS221_U4_T2#GNS221_U4_T2_h7)
